{{smaller block|<poem>''Whenever'' you have need,
You may be armed and appointed well.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Tit. And., iv. 2. 15.}}}}

'''whenne<sup>1</sup>†''', ''adv.'' An obsolete form of ''when''.

'''whenne<sup>2</sup>†''', ''adv.'' and ''conj.'' [< ME. ''whenne, hwenne, hwanene, whanene, wonene, wanene, hwenene,'' etc., < AS. ''hwanan, hwanon, hwonan'' (= OS. ''hvanen, hvanan'' = OHG. ''wanana, wannan,'' MHG. G. ''wannen,'' whence); with adv. formative ''-an,'' < ''hwænne,'' etc., when: see ''when''. Cf. ''hence, thence,'' similarly formed.] '''I.''' ''interrog. adv.'' Whence?

'''II.''' ''rel. conj.'' Whence.

{{smaller block|Sei me hwet art thu ant ''hweonne'' ant hwa the hider sende.
{{right|''St. Juliana'' (E. E. T. S.), p. 38.}}}}

'''whennes†''', ''adv.'' and ''conj.'' A Middle English form of ''whence''.

'''whenso''' (hwen-sō′), ''adv.'' [< ME. ''whenso, hwense;'' < ''when'' + ''so''<sup>1</sup>.] When; whenever. ''Old Eng. Homilies'' (ed. Morris), I. 85. [Archaic.]

{{smaller block|In a far-off land is their dwelling, ''whenso'' they sit at home.
{{right|''W. Morris,'' quoted in The Academy, Feb. 9, 1889, p. 85.}}}}

'''whensoever''' (hwen-sọ̄-ev′ėr), ''conj.'' [< ''when'' + ''so''<sup>1</sup> + ''ever''.] At what time soever; at whatever time.

{{smaller block|Mercifully assist our prayers which we make before thee in all our troubles and adversities, ''whensoever'' they oppress us.
{{right|''Book of Common Prayer,'' Lesser Litany.}}}}

'''wher<sup>1</sup>†''', ''adv.'' and ''conj.'' See ''where''<sup>1</sup>.

'''wher<sup>2</sup>†''', ''conj.'' See ''where''<sup>2</sup>.

{{RunningHeader|wheme|6893|whereabout}}{{nop}}'''wheme†''', ''a.'' and ''v.'' An obsolete variant of ''queme.'' '''whemmel, whemmle''' (hwem′l), ''v. t.''   [Also ''whammel'', Sc. ''quhemle'', ''whamle'', ''whommel'', a freq. (or perhaps orig. transposed) form of ''whelm.'']   To whelm. [Prov. Eng. and Scotch.] '''whemmel, whemmle''' (hwem′l), ''n.'' An overturn; an overthrow. [Scotch.] {{smaller block|Nae doubt — ay, ay — it ’s an awfu’ ''whummle'' — and for ane that held his head sae high, too. {{right|''Scott'', Rob Roy, xxii.}}}} '''when''' (hwen), ''adv.'' and ''conj.''   [< ME. ''when'', ''whan'', ''whon'', ''qvan'', ''qven'', ''qwan'', ''wan'', ''won'', ''hwon'', ''whenne'', ''whanne'', ''hwenne'', ''hwanne'', ''hwonne'', ''wenne'', ''wanne'', ''wonne'', ''wane'', ''wone'', < AS. ''hwænne'', ''hwonne'', when, = OS. ''hwan'' = OFries. ''hwenne'' = MD. ''wan'' = OHG. MHG. ''wanne'', ''hwanne'', G. ''wann'', when, ''wenn'', when, if, = Goth. ''hwan'', when; orig. a case of the interrog. pron. (cf. Goth. ''hwana'', acc. masc.), Goth. ''hwas'' = AS. ''hwā'', etc., who? see ''who''. Cf. L. ''quum'', ''quom'', when, as related to L. ''quis'', who? Gr. πότε, when? from same pron. base. Hence ult. ''whenne''2, ''whence''.]   '''I.''' ''interrog. adv.'' At what time? at which time? {{smaller block|''When'' shall these things be? and what shall be the sign of thy coming? {{right|Mat. xxiv. 3.}}}} {{smaller block|One [window] to the west, and counter to it, And blank; and who shall blazon it? ''when'' and how?{{right|''Tennyson'', Holy Grail.}}}} {{smaller block|''When'' was formerly used exclamatorily, like ''what'', to express impatience.}} {{smaller block|Why, ''when'', I say? . . . Off with my boots, you rogues! you villains, ''when?'' . . . Out, you rogue! you pluck my foot awry.{{right|''Shak.'', T. of the S., iv. 1. 146.}}}} {{smaller block|Why, ''when?'' begin, sir: I must stay your leisure.{{right|''Middleton'', More Dissemblers besides Women, v. 1.}}}} Set, parson, set; the dice die in my hand. ''When'', parson, ''when!'' what, can you find no more? {{smaller block|{{right|''Munday'' (''and others''), Sir John Oldcastle, iv. 1.}}}} '''II.''' ''rel. conj.'' '''1.''' At the or any time that; at or just after the moment that; as soon as. {{smaller block|''Whan'' Gawein saugh hem come, he seide now may we a-bide to longe. {{right|''Merlin'' (E. E. T. S.), iii. 587.}}}} {{smaller block|''When'' the broken arches are black in night, And each shafted oriel glimmers white, . . . Then view St. David’s ruin’d pile. {{right|''Scott'', L. of L. M., ii. 1.}}}} '''2.''' At which time. {{smaller block|I am at London only to provide for Monday, ''when'' I shall use that favour which my Lady Bedford hath afforded me, of giving her name to my daughter. {{right|''Donne'', Letters, xiii.}}}} {{smaller block|The Moors fought valiantly for a short time, until the alcaydes of Marabella and Casares were slain, ''when'' they gave way and fled for the rear-guard. {{right|''Irving'', Granada, p. 79.}}}} {{smaller block|A time ''when'' the idols of the market-place are more devoutly worshipped than ever Diana of the Ephesians was. {{right|''Lowell'', Harvard Anniversary.}}}} {{smaller block|''When'' in this sense is sometimes used with ellipsis of ''the time'' preceding.}} {{smaller block|I knew ''when'' seven justices could not take up a quarrel. {{right|''Shak.'', As you Like it, v. 4. 103.}}}} {{smaller block|They were apprehended, and expected euer ''when'' to be put to death. Quoted in ''Capt. John Smith’s'' Works, I. 213.}} '''3.''' At the same time that; whereas; while on the contrary: used adversatively, to denote contrast or incompatibility. {{smaller block|You rub the sore, ''When'' you should bring the plaster. {{right|''Shak.'', Tempest, ii. 1. 139.}}}} {{smaller block|How shall I please thee, how deserve thy smiles, ''When'' I am only rich in misery? {{right|''Beau. and Fl.'', Knight of Burning Pestle, ii. 2.}}}} {{smaller block|How then can any man be as a Witness, ''when'' every man is made the Accuser? {{right|''Selden'', Table-Talk, p. 38.}}}} {{smaller|''When'' was formerly followed by ''as'' and ''that'' used redundantly. See ''whenas.''}} {{smaller block|''Whan that'' Aprille with his shoures soote The droghte of Marche hath perced to the roote. {{right|''Chaucer'', Gen. Prol. to C. T., l. 1.}}}} {{smaller block|''Qwene that'' the kynge Arthur by conqueste hade wonnyne Castelles and kyngdoms, and contreez many. {{right|''Morte Arthure'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 26.}}}} {{smaller|''When'' is often used as a quasi-pronoun, meaning ‘which time,’ introducing a dependent clause after ''since, till'', or similar connective denoting time.}} {{smaller block|Shortly . . . I’ll resolve you, . . . These happen’d accidents; ''till when'', be cheerful. {{right|''Shak.'', Tempest, v. 1. 250.}}}} {{smaller block|''Since when'', his brain that had before been dry, Became the well-spring of all poetry. {{right|''Sir J. Davies'', Dancing.}}}} {{smaller block|Thy steeds will pause at even — ''till when'', farewell. {{right|''Shelley'', Prometheus Unbound, iii. 2.}}}} '''When all comes to all.''' See ''all.'' '''whenas''' (hwen-az′), ''conj.''   [< ''when'' + ''as''1.]   '''1.''' When. [Archaic.] {{smaller block|Come, give me now a bag for my bread, . . . And one for a peny, ''whenas'' I get any. {{right|''Little John and the Four Beggars'' (Child’s Ballads, V. 326).}}}} {{smaller block|''Whenas'' in silks my Julia goes, Till then, methinks, how sweetly flows That liquefaction of her clothes! {{right|''Herrick'', Upon Julia’s Clothes.}}}} 433 '''2.''' Whereas; while. [Rare.] {{smaller block|''Whenas,'' if they would enquire into themselves, they would find no such matter. {{right|''Barrow.''}}}} {{smaller block|Fit professors indeed are they like to be to teach others that godlinesse with content is great gaine, ''whenas'' their godlinesse of teaching had not been but for worldly gaine. {{right|''Milton'', On Def. of Humb. Remonst.}}}} '''whence''' (hwens), ''adv.'' and ''conj.''   [< ME. ''whens'', ''whennes'', ''whannes'', ''huannes'', with adv. gen. ''-es'', < ''whenne'', whence: see ''whenne''2.]   '''I.''' ''interrog. adv.'' From what place? from what source, origin, or antecedents? {{smaller block|''First Outlaw. Whence'' came you?
''Val.'' From Milan. {{right|''Shak.'', T. G. of V., iv. 1. 18.}}}} '''II.''' ''rel. conj.'' From what place; from which place or source. {{smaller block|Thes gost [spirit] him sseweth huet he is, . . . and ''huannes'' he comth, and huyder he geth. {{right|''Ayenbite of Inwyt'' (E. E. T. S.), p. 115.}}}} {{smaller block|I wot wel what ȝe ar & ''whennes'' ȝe come. {{right|''William of Palerne'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 3122.}}}} {{smaller block|Look unto the rock ''whence'' ye are hewn, and to the hole of the pit ''whence'' ye are digged. {{right|Isa. li. 1.}}}} {{smaller block|Now wee may perceave the root of his hatred ''whence'' it springs. {{right|''Milton'', Eikonoklastes, iv.}}}} {{smaller block|We know not ''whence'' we live, Or why, or how. {{right|''Shelley'', Revolt of Islam, ix. 33.}}}} {{smaller block|Here was square keep, there turret high, . . . ''Whence'' oft the Warder could descry The gathering ocean-storm. {{right|''Scott'', Marmion, v. 33.}}}} '''From whence''', whence: a common pleonasm. {{smaller block|''From whence'' come wars and fightings among ye? {{right|Jas. iv. 1.}}}} {{smaller block|A place ''From whence'' himself does fly. {{right|''Shak.'', Macbeth, iv. 2. 8.}}}} {{smaller block|O, how unlike the place ''from whence'' they fell. {{right|''Milton'', P. L., i. 75.}}}} '''Of whence''', whence: a pleonasm. [Rare.] {{smaller block|He asked his airy guide, What and ''of whence'' was he, who pressed the hero’s side. {{right|''Dryden'', Æneid, vi. 1193.}}}} '''whence-ever''' (hwens-ev′ėr), ''conj.''   [< ''whence'' + ''ever.'']   Whencesoever.   ''Prior.'' (''Worcester.'') [Rare.] '''whenceforth†''' (hwens-fōrth′), ''conj.''   [< ''whence'' + ''forth''1.]   Forth from which place; whence. [Rare.] {{smaller block|Before them stands the God of Seas in place, . . . And strikes the rockes with his three-forked mace; ''Whenceforth'' issues a warlike steed in sight. {{right|''Spenser'', Muiopotmos, l. 316.}}}} '''whencesoever''' (hwens-sō-ev′ėr), ''conj.''   [Early mod. E. ''whens-soever''; < ''whence'' + ''so''1 + ''ever.'']   From what place soever; from what cause or source soever. {{smaller block|This Cytie of Jherusalem is in a fayre emynent place, for it stondeth vpon suche a grounde that from ''whens soever'' a man commyth thede he must nede ascende. {{right|''Sir R. Guylforde'', Pylgrymage, p. 22.}}}} {{smaller block|Any idea, ''whencesoever'' we have it. {{right|''Locke.''}}}} '''whene’er''' (hwen-ãr′), ''conj.'' A contracted form of ''whenever.'' '''whenever''' (hwen-ev′ėr), ''conj.''   [< ME. ''when ever''; < ''when'' + ''ever.'']   At whatever time; at what time soever. {{smaller block|Ser, on to hir loggyng, ''When euer'' it please yow, I shall be your gyde; ffor she is here by vppon the Ryuerez side. {{right|''Generydes'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 1245.}}}} ''Whenever'' you have need, You may be armed and appointed well. {{smaller block|{{right|''Shak.'', Tit. And., iv. 2. 15.}}}} '''whenne1†''', ''adv.'' An obsolete form of ''when''. '''whenne2†''', ''adv.'' and ''conj.''   [< ME. ''whenne, hwenne, hwanene, whanene, wonene, wanene, hwenene,'' etc., < AS. ''hwanan, hwanon, hwonan'' (= OS. ''hvanen, hvanan'' = OHG. ''wanana, wannan,'' MHG. G. ''wannen,'' whence); with adv. formative ''-an,'' < ''hwænne,'' etc., when: see ''when''. Cf. ''hence, thence,'' similarly formed.]   '''I.''' ''interrog. adv.'' Whence? '''II.''' ''rel. conj.'' Whence. {{smaller block|Sei me hwet art thu ant ''hweonne'' ant hwa the hider sende. {{right|''St. Juliana'' (E. E. T. S.), p. 38.}}}} '''whennes†''', ''adv.'' and ''conj.'' A Middle English form of ''whence''. '''whenso''' (hwen-sō′), ''adv.''   [< ME. ''whenso, hwense;'' < ''when'' + ''so''1.]   When; whenever. ''Old Eng. Homilies'' (ed. Morris), I. 85. [Archaic.] {{smaller block|In a far-off land is their dwelling, ''whenso'' they sit at home. {{right|''W. Morris,'' quoted in The Academy, Feb. 9, 1889, p. 85.}}}} '''whensoever''' (hwen-sọ̄-ev′ėr), ''conj.''   [< ''when'' + ''so''1 + ''ever''.]   At what time soever; at whatever time. {{smaller block|Mercifully assist our prayers which we make before thee in all our troubles and adversities, ''whensoever'' they oppress us. {{right|''Book of Common Prayer,'' Lesser Litany.}}}} '''wher1†''', ''adv.'' and ''conj.'' See ''where''1. '''wher2†''', ''conj.'' See ''where''2. '''where1''' (hwãr), ''adv.'' and ''conj.''   [< ME. ''wher, whar, whær, ware, war, wor, hwere, hware, hwar, hwær'', < AS. ''hwær'', ''hwār'' = OS. ''hwār'', ''huār'' = OFries. ''hwēr'' = D. ''waar'' = MLG. ''wār'', ''wōr'', LG. ''waar'', ''woor'' = OHG. ''wār'', ''hwār'', MHG. ''wār-'', G. ''war-'' (in comp., as in ''war-um'', ''wor-in''), also reduced, OHG. MHG. ''wā'', G. ''wo'' = Icel. Sw. ''hvar'' = Dan. ''hvor'' = Goth. ''hwar'', where?; cf. Lith. ''kur'', where? L. ''cur'', OL. ''quor'', sometimes ''cor'' (usually explained as a contraction of ''quā re''), why? Skt. ''karhi'', at what time? when?; from the pronominal base represented by ''who'', ''what'': see ''who'', ''what''1. Cf. ''there'', as related to ''the'', ''that''.]   '''I.''' ''interrog. adv.'' '''1.''' At or in what place? in what position, situation, or circumstances? {{smaller block|''Hwer'' scule [shall] we win [wine] finden? {{right|''Old Eng. Hom.'' (ed. Morris), I. 241.}}}} {{smaller block|If there were no opposition, ''where'' were the triall of an unfained goodnesse and magnanimity? {{right|''Milton'', Church-Government, i. 7.}}}} {{smaller block|''Where'' sooner than here, ''where'' louder than here, may we expect a patriotic voice to be raised? {{right|''D. Webster'', Speech, New York, March 10, 1831.}}}} '''2.''' To which place? whither? {{smaller block|''Where'' is bicome Cesar, that lorde was of al; Or the riche man clothid in purpur & in pal? {{right|''Hymns to Virgin'', etc. (E. E. T. S.), p. 86.}}}} {{smaller block|''Where'' runn’st thou so fast? {{right|''Shak.'', C. of E., iii. 2. 71.}}}} '''3.''' From what source? whence? {{smaller block|''Where'' have they this mettle? Is not their climate foggy, raw and dull? {{right|''Shak.'', Hen. V., iii. 5. 15.}}}} {{smaller|'''Where away?''' (''naut.''), a query from the officer of the deck as to the direction of any object reported by the lookout.}} '''II.''' ''rel. conj.'' '''1.''' At or in which place, or the place in which; in which case, position, circumstances, etc. {{smaller block|Asketh him Hwat beo ordre, and ''hwar'' he ifinde in holi write religiun openluker descriued. {{right|''Ancren Riwle'', p. 8.}}}} {{smaller block|He enforces hym to seke Ihesu in the joy of the worlde, ''whare'' neuer he sall be fundene. {{right|''Hampole'', Prose Treatises (E. E. T. S.), p. 5.}}}} {{smaller block|Bare ruin’d choirs, ''where'' late the sweet birds sang. {{right|''Shak.'', Sonnets, lxxiii.}}}} '''2.''' To which place; whither; to a place such that. {{smaller block|Oh, cousin! thou hast led me ''where'' I never Shall see day more. ''Shirley'', The Wedding, ii. 2.}} '''3.''' Wherever. {{smaller block|''Where'' the lordes and cheif men wax soe barbarous and bastardlike, what shall be hoped of the pesantes? {{right|''Spenser'', State of Ireland.}}}} {{smaller block|''Where'' your treasure is, there will your heart be also. {{right|Mat. vi. 21.}}}} {{smaller block|Now ''where'' nothing is, there nothing can come to be. {{right|''J. Behme'', Aurora, xix. 438.}}}} '''4.''' Whereas. {{smaller block|His [Armagnac’s] wealth doth warrant a liberal dower, ''Where'' Reignier sooner will receive than give. {{right|''Shak.'', 1 Hen. VI., v. 5. 47.}}}} {{smaller block|It was observed that those who were born after the Beginning of this Mortality [the plague] had but twenty-eight Teeth, ''where'' before they had two and thirty. {{right|''Baker'', Chronicles, p. 131.}}}} {{smaller block|''Where'', frequently having the force or function of a relative or other pronoun (''which'', ''what'', etc.), is often used in composition with a following preposition: as, ''whereby'', ‘by what,’ ‘by which’; ''wherewith'', ‘with what,’ ‘with which.’ It was also formerly used after certain adverbs or adjectives in a general sense, as it still is in ''everywhere'', ''somewhere'' (which see), Middle English ''widen-wher'' (astray, at random), in forms corresponding to similar compounds of ''there'' (see ''there'').}} {{smaller block|Thus I wente ''wyden-wher'', Dowel to seche. {{right|''Piers Plowman'' (A), ix. 53.}}}} '''where'''1'''†''' (hwãr), ''n.''   [Formerly also ''wheare;'' < ''where''1, ''adv.'', as used in ''everywhere, somewhere.'']   Whereabout; situation; place. {{smaller block|Finding the Nymph asleepe in secret ''wheare.'' {{right|''Spenser'', F. Q., III. iv. 19.}}}} {{smaller block|Bid them farewell, Cordelia, though unkind: Thou losest here, a better ''where'' to find. {{right|''Shak.'', Lear, i. 1. 264.}}}} '''where'''2'''†''', ''conj.''   [< ME. ''wher, where'', contraction of ''wheder'', E. ''whether''1.]   A contracted form of ''whether''1. {{smaller block|''Wher'' he [the cat] ryt other rest other romyth to playe. {{right|''Piers Plowman'' (C), i. 186.}}}} {{smaller block|Off hir linage enquered I no-thing; ''Where'' she be of duk or of markois hy, Forsoth I wyll hyr haue, she is me pleasyng. {{right|''Rom. of Partenay'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 850.}}}} {{smaller block|I know not ''whēr'' I am or no; or speak, Or whether thou dost hear me. {{right|''B. Jonson'', New Inn, v. 1.}}}} '''whereabout''' (hwãr′a-bout′), ''adv.'' and ''conj.''   [< ''where''1 + ''about.'']   '''I.''' ''interrog. adv.'' About what? concerning what? near what or which place? as, ''whereabout'' did you drop the coin? '''II.''' ''rel. conj.'' About which; concerning which; on what purpose. {{smaller block|Let no man know anything of the business ''whereabout'' I send thee. {{right|1 Sam. xxi. 2.}}}} {{smaller block|I must not have you henceforth question me Whither I go, nor reason ''whereabout.'' {{right|''Shak.'', 1 Hen. IV., ii. 3. 107.}}}}
